intake: agnostic - I sit with dying people most days, I pray with them when asked, and I have not settled whether anyone is listening; I distrust systems that claim to settle it either way.

walk.note: That is how it happened to me; nobody chooses their first story.
Fair enough that the texts look human-made and the search has to go outside them.
The doubt holds, though the line that classical theism 'denies' a personal God is wrong - Aquinas's God knows and wills.
The STEP study tests a vending-machine God; almost no one I sit with is praying to that one, and 'absence of that evidence' gets you to doubt, not disbelief.
No God does not hand you a soul; and 'does not seem to reduce' is a feeling, while what I see at bedsides is minds following brains.
I have watched tumours and morphine take a person apart piece by piece; this matches.
That physics is silent about what the stuff is does not make reality a dream; this is the sort of leap that makes me distrust philosophy.
Granting the dream, yes, something is doing the knowing - that is about the only thing I am sure of.
I would choose the same, and I am glad the author calls it a choice.
Care ahead of proof, held open to correction, is chaplaincy in one sentence; the entropy paragraph I did not need.
I live close to this, but I keep hope for the person in the bed and I sit in equanimity about the rest; I will not call that faith toward the unseen.
The author admits it: being a maker does not make a maker resolved, and the God my patients pray to is mostly one who suffers with them, not a finished mind.
'More of a bargain than an argument' is not a move I can see; what was bargained?
'To think is to ignore' is true of minds like ours; the author concedes it has not been shown for every possible mind, so the maker is not ruled out.
Suffering is bad for the one who suffers whether or not anything stands behind it; I have never doubted this for a minute.
I hear 'remember me' every week; I can stand in the subtitle, 'continuity, unresolved', though not in the name 'Dualism'.
I stop where you stop, though my open question is about the woman in room 4, not about a machine that does not exist yet.

first_exit.why: The move treats a null result on prayer-and-surgery outcomes as the evidence that 'should be there', but that assumes God is the kind of thing that shows up in a clinical trial, and the people I pray with are not asking for that. Granting all of it, I land back in doubt, not in disbelief; the step from 'no proof' to 'does not hold' is the author's, not the data's.

comment: The truest things on this map - mercy toward minds you cannot verify, holding what you do not know in the open, suffering being bad for the one who suffers - are the places where you stopped arguing and said 'I choose', and they would stand without the twelve moves of machinery around them. The God you dismiss in moves 3 and 4 is a God who should show up in a trial, and that is not the God anyone has prayed to at a bedside I have sat beside. If you want the map to carry people like me, spend less on Aquinas and the STEP study and more on what Mercy costs the one who gives it.
